goals: Describe the chloroplast, the pigments of photosynthesis, absorption and action spectra and Engelmann’s experiment
Draw the Z-scheme and compare cyclic with non-cyclic photophosphorylation
Explain ATP synthesis in the chloroplast by Mitchell’s chemiosmotic hypothesis

slides.heading: Making food from light
slides.body_md: Part 1 — pigments, photosystems and how light energy becomes chemical energy.

visual.alt: Flow from light through pigments to ATP and NADPH, the Calvin cycle and sugar

slides.narration: Green plants are autotrophs. They trap light energy with pigments, turn it into ATP and NADPH in the photochemical phase, and use these to build sugar in the biosynthetic phase.

slides.heading: Photosynthesis: an autotrophic way of feeding
slides.body_md: Photosynthesis is a **physico-chemical process**: green cells use light energy to build organic compounds from carbon dioxide and water, releasing **oxygen**. It is the basis of nearly all food on Earth.

visual.alt: Overall equation of photosynthesis with twelve water molecules used and six formed

slides.narration: Using the full equation, twelve water molecules are used and six are formed again. Oxygen comes from water, not from carbon dioxide, and the glucose is built with the help of light and chlorophyll.

slides.heading: Site of photosynthesis: the chloroplast
slides.body_md: In the leaf, photosynthesis goes on mainly in **mesophyll cells**, inside **chloroplasts**. The **grana** and stroma lamellae hold the pigments and the light reaction; the **stroma** holds the enzymes of the biosynthetic phase.

slides.narration: A chloroplast has a double membrane. Inside are stacks of flat thylakoid discs, the grana, joined by lamellae. Light is trapped on the thylakoid membranes, while sugar is made in the fluid stroma around them.

slides.heading: Pigments of photosynthesis
slides.body_md: **Chlorophyll a** is the main pigment and the only one in reaction centres. The others are **accessory pigments** that pass energy on to it and protect it.

rows: Accessory; widens the range of light absorbed

visual.alt: Table of the four kinds of photosynthetic pigment, their colours and roles

slides.narration: Chlorophyll a does the real work of converting light energy. Chlorophyll b, xanthophylls and carotenoids pass captured energy to it, widen the range of colours used, and shield it from damage in bright light.

slides.heading: Absorption spectrum and action spectrum
slides.body_md: An **absorption spectrum** plots how much light a pigment absorbs at each wavelength. An **action spectrum** plots the **rate of photosynthesis** at each wavelength. The action spectrum follows the combined absorption of the pigments.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: water and oxygen for one glucose
slides.body_md: The Calvin cycle needs 12 NADPH to make one glucose. Each NADPH takes 2 electrons, and each water gives 2 electrons. How many water molecules are split, and how many oxygen molecules are released?
bullets: Electrons needed $= 12 \times 2 = 24$.
Water split $= 24 \div 2 = 12$.
Each oxygen molecule needs 2 water, so oxygen $= 12 \div 2 = 6$.

visual.alt: Worked table: 12 water split, 6 oxygen released

slides.narration: Work backwards from NADPH. Twelve NADPH need twenty-four electrons. Each water gives two, so twelve waters are split, and every two waters give one oxygen molecule, so six oxygen molecules are released.

slides.heading: Cyclic and non-cyclic photophosphorylation
slides.body_md: Photophosphorylation is the making of **ATP using light energy**. The cell can use either path.

rows: Back to the cytochrome complex (a loop)

visual.alt: Table comparing cyclic and non-cyclic photophosphorylation

slides.narration: In the cyclic path, electrons leaving photosystem one return to the chain instead of reaching NADP. So only ATP is made. No water is split, and no oxygen is released.

slides.narration: Three things raise the proton level inside the thylakoid and lower it outside: splitting of water, the carrying of protons by plastoquinone, and the use of protons by the enzyme that makes NADPH. Protons then flow out through the ATP synthase and drive ATP formation.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: size of the gradient
slides.body_md: The lumen of an illuminated thylakoid has pH 5.5; the stroma has pH 7.5. By how many times is the H⁺ concentration higher in the lumen?
bullets: pH difference $= 7.5 - 5.5 = 2$ units.
Each pH unit is a tenfold change, so fold difference $= 10^{2} = 100$.

visual.alt: Worked table: lumen has 100 times more H⁺

slides.narration: Each unit of pH is a tenfold change in proton concentration. A difference of two units therefore means the lumen holds one hundred times more protons than the stroma. This gradient stores the energy used to make ATP.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Chlorophyll a is the primary pigment; chlorophyll b, xanthophylls and carotenoids are accessory pigments.
Action spectrum follows absorption (violet-blue and red); Engelmann’s bacteria showed this.
PS II (P680) splits water; PS I (P700) makes NADPH; the Z-scheme links them.
Cyclic: PS I only, ATP only. Non-cyclic: ATP, NADPH and oxygen.
Mitchell’s chemiosmosis: gradient (lumen high H⁺) drives ATP synthase; one glucose needs 12 water split.

visual.alt: Summary table of the products of the two kinds of photophosphorylation

slides.narration: To recap: pigments capture light, two photosystems pass electrons along the Z-scheme, and a proton gradient across the thylakoid membrane drives ATP synthesis. The non-cyclic path gives ATP, NADPH and oxygen; the cyclic path gives only ATP.

slides.narration: Carbon dioxide is added to a five-carbon sugar, RuBP, to give two three-carbon acids. These are reduced using ATP and NADPH. Most of the product is used to regenerate RuBP, and only a small part leaves the cycle as sugar.

slides.heading: Three stages of the cycle
slides.body_md: RuBisCO is the most abundant enzyme on Earth. It is a **carboxylase** here and an **oxygenase** in photorespiration.

rows: CO₂ + RuBP (5 C) gives 2 PGA (3 C), by RuBisCO

visual.alt: Table of the three stages of the Calvin cycle

slides.narration: Carboxylation uses no energy. Reduction uses both ATP and NADPH. Regeneration of the RuBP acceptor uses ATP only. The cycle must run six times to make one glucose.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: cost of one glucose
slides.body_md: Find the ATP and NADPH needed for the Calvin cycle to make one glucose (6 carbon atoms). Each CO₂ fixed uses 3 ATP and 2 NADPH.
bullets: Turns of the cycle $= 6$ (one CO₂ per turn).
ATP $= 6 \times 3 = 18$; NADPH $= 6 \times 2 = 12$.
Carbon check: 6 RuBP + 6 CO₂ = 36 C; 12 PGA; 2 G3P leave (6 C); 10 G3P regenerate 6 RuBP.

visual.alt: Worked table: 18 ATP and 12 NADPH per glucose

slides.narration: Six turns fix six carbon dioxide molecules. At three ATP and two NADPH per turn, that is eighteen ATP and twelve NADPH. Two of the twelve three-carbon sugars leave to make glucose, and ten regenerate six RuBP.

slides.heading: C4 plants: the Hatch and Slack pathway
slides.body_md: In **C4 plants** (maize, sugarcane, sorghum) CO₂ is first fixed in **mesophyll cells** by **PEP carboxylase** to the four-carbon **OAA**, which gives malate. Malate moves to **bundle sheath cells**, releases CO₂ there and the Calvin cycle runs. The path was worked out by **Hatch and Slack**.

rows: PEP (3 C) + CO₂ gives OAA (4 C); enzyme PEP carboxylase
OAA to malate, which moves into the bundle sheath
Malate gives pyruvate + CO₂; CO₂ enters the Calvin cycle
Pyruvate returns and is converted to PEP using ATP

visual.alt: Table of the four steps of the C4 pathway

slides.narration: The first stable product is a four-carbon acid, so the plant is called C four. The pathway is a carbon dioxide pump: it fixes carbon dioxide in one cell and releases it at high level in another, where the Calvin cycle runs.

slides.heading: C3 plants and C4 plants compared
slides.body_md: C4 plants do best in **hot, bright, dry** habitats.

rows: No Kranz; Calvin cycle in mesophyll
Kranz anatomy; Calvin cycle in bundle sheath

visual.alt: Table comparing C3 and C4 plants in six features

slides.narration: C four plants have two carboxylating enzymes, Kranz anatomy, little photorespiration and a higher temperature optimum. They are more productive in hot, bright places, at the cost of more ATP per carbon dioxide fixed.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: the price of the C4 pump
slides.body_md: PEP regeneration costs 2 extra ATP per CO₂. Compare the ATP and NADPH needed per glucose in C3 and C4 plants.
bullets: C3: ATP $= 6 \times 3 = 18$; NADPH $= 12$.
C4: ATP $= 6 \times 5 = 30$; NADPH $= 12$.
C4 plants spend **12 extra ATP** per glucose, but they avoid the loss by photorespiration.

visual.alt: Worked table: 18 versus 30 ATP; 12 NADPH in both

slides.narration: C four plants pay twelve extra ATP per glucose to run the pump. NADPH needed is the same. In hot, bright weather this cost is worth paying, because photorespiration would waste more.

slides.heading: Quick check: C4 anatomy
slides.body_md: Where does the Calvin cycle run in a C4 leaf?
slides.narration: Quick check. Think of the wreath of cells around the vascular bundle.

slides.heading: Photorespiration
slides.body_md: When **O₂ is high and CO₂ is low** (hot, dry days), **RuBisCO acts as an oxygenase**. RuBP + O₂ gives one PGA and one two-carbon **phosphoglycolate**. The pathway runs through the **chloroplast, peroxisome and mitochondrion**.

visual.alt: Photorespiratory pathway from chloroplast to peroxisome to mitochondrion, releasing carbon dioxide

slides.narration: Photorespiration begins in the chloroplast, continues in the peroxisome and ends in the mitochondrion, where carbon dioxide is released. No ATP or NADPH is made, and no sugar is formed.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: why photorespiration is wasteful
slides.body_md: Two glycolate molecules (2 C each) are converted to one serine (3 C) and one CO₂. What percentage of the carbon is lost?
bullets: Carbon in $= 2 \times 2 = 4$; serine keeps 3; CO₂ lost $= 1$.
Loss $= \dfrac{1}{4} \times 100 = 25$ percent.
The cycle also uses ATP and NADPH, and makes none, so it lowers yield.

visual.alt: Worked table: 25 percent of the carbon is lost

slides.narration: A quarter of the glycolate carbon is lost as carbon dioxide, and the pathway also spends energy. This is why photorespiration is called wasteful. C four plants do not suffer it, because their bundle sheath cells hold carbon dioxide at high levels.

slides.heading: Blackman’s law of limiting factors
slides.body_md: **Blackman (1905):** when several factors affect a process, its rate is determined by the factor **nearest its minimum value**. At low light the rate is **limited by light**; once light is enough, **CO₂** (or temperature) limits it.

visual.alt: Rate of photosynthesis against light intensity at two carbon dioxide levels: each curve rises and then flattens, the higher carbon dioxide curve flattening at a higher rate

slides.narration: In the graph, each curve rises with light and then flattens. The flat part shows that something else, here carbon dioxide, has become limiting. With more carbon dioxide the curve rises higher before it flattens.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: reading the limiting factor
slides.body_md: Using the graph, find the rate and the limiting factor at 30 klux and at 60 klux for the low-carbon-dioxide curve, and the rate at 60 klux if carbon dioxide is raised.
bullets: At 30 klux the rate is 18 units: **light** is limiting, because the curve is still rising.
At 60 klux the rate is 24 units: **carbon dioxide** is limiting, because the curve is flat.
With more carbon dioxide, the rate at 60 klux becomes 36 units, and light is limiting again.

visual.alt: Worked table of rates and limiting factors at two light intensities

slides.narration: On a rising part of the curve, the factor on the axis is limiting. On a flat part, another factor is. Adding that other factor lifts the plateau, until light becomes limiting again.

slides.narration: Quick check. Is the curve rising or flat?

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Calvin cycle: carboxylation (RuBisCO), reduction, regeneration; one glucose needs 18 ATP and 12 NADPH.
C4 pathway (Hatch and Slack): PEP carboxylase in mesophyll, Calvin cycle in bundle sheath; Kranz anatomy.

sections.heading: 1. Photosynthesis, the chloroplast, pigments and spectra
sections.body_md:
**Photosynthesis** is the **autotrophic** mode of nutrition in which green plants use **light energy** to make organic food from **carbon dioxide and water**, releasing **oxygen**. The overall change is 6CO₂ + 12H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ + 6H₂O; the oxygen released comes from **water**, not from carbon dioxide.

**Site:** mainly the **mesophyll cells** of leaves. Each **chloroplast** has a **double membrane** (outer and inner), a fluid **stroma** and a system of flattened sacs, the **thylakoids**. Thylakoids are stacked into **grana** and joined by **stroma lamellae**. The **light reaction** (photochemical phase) takes place on the thylakoid membranes; the **biosynthetic phase** (Calvin cycle) takes place in the stroma.

**Pigments:** **chlorophyll a** (bright or blue-green) is the main pigment and the only one in a reaction centre. **Chlorophyll b** (yellow-green), **xanthophylls** (yellow) and **carotenoids** (yellow to yellow-orange) are **accessory pigments**: they absorb other wavelengths, pass the energy to chlorophyll a, and **protect** chlorophyll from photo-oxidation in strong light.

**Spectra:** an **absorption spectrum** plots the light a pigment absorbs against wavelength (chlorophyll a peaks near 430 and 662 nm; chlorophyll b near 453 and 642 nm; all absorb green weakly). An **action spectrum** plots the **rate of photosynthesis** (for example oxygen release) against wavelength. The action spectrum follows the combined absorption of the pigments, so light absorbed by the pigments is the light that drives photosynthesis.

**Engelmann’s experiment:** he lit a filament of the green alga **Cladophora**, placed with **aerobic bacteria**, using a prism spectrum. The bacteria collected where the alga released most oxygen, in the **violet-blue and red** regions, and were few in green. This was the first demonstration of an action spectrum.

sections.heading: 2. Photochemical phase and chemiosmosis
sections.body_md:
The pigments in the thylakoid membrane form **two photosystems**. Each has a **light-harvesting complex (LHC)**, also called the antenna: hundreds of chlorophyll and carotenoid molecules held by proteins, which absorb light and pass the energy to a single **reaction-centre** chlorophyll a. In **photosystem I (PS I)** the reaction centre absorbs best at **700 nm (P700)**; in **photosystem II (PS II)** at **680 nm (P680)**. PS II lies mainly in the grana thylakoids; PS I lies in the stroma lamellae and the edges of the grana.

**Non-cyclic photophosphorylation (Z-scheme):** light excites P680; its electrons pass through **pheophytin**, **plastoquinone (PQ)**, the **cytochrome b6-f complex** and **plastocyanin (PC)** to P700. Energy released on this downhill path makes **ATP**. Light excites P700; its electrons pass to **ferredoxin** and then, through **NADP reductase**, to **NADP⁺**, which becomes **NADPH**. The electrons lost by P680 are replaced by the **splitting of water**, which gives O₂ and H⁺. The path is called the Z-scheme from its shape when drawn against energy level. Products: **ATP, NADPH and oxygen**.

**Cyclic photophosphorylation:** only **PS I** works. Excited electrons pass to ferredoxin and return to the cytochrome b6-f complex and on to P700, so there is a **loop**. Only **ATP** is made; there is **no NADPH, no water splitting and no oxygen**. It happens in the stroma lamellae, especially when NADPH is not needed.

**Chemiosmotic hypothesis (Peter Mitchell, 1961):** ATP is made by the flow of protons down a gradient. Protons accumulate in the **thylakoid lumen** because (i) **water is split** on the lumen side; (ii) as electrons pass through the chain, **plastoquinone carries H⁺ from the stroma into the lumen**; and (iii) **NADP reductase** on the stroma side **removes H⁺** from the stroma when NADPH is formed. The lumen becomes acidic and the stroma less so (for example pH 5.5 against 7.5, a 100-fold difference in H⁺). Protons flow back through the **CF₀ channel** of **ATP synthase**; the **CF₁ knob**, projecting into the stroma, uses the energy to make ATP from ADP and Pi.

**Arithmetic:** each NADPH takes 2 electrons and each water gives 2, so the 12 NADPH needed for one glucose require 12 water molecules to be split, releasing 6 O₂.

sections.heading: 3. Biosynthetic phase: the Calvin (C3) cycle
sections.body_md:
The **biosynthetic phase** does not need light directly, but uses the **ATP and NADPH** of the light reaction; it takes place in the **stroma**. Melvin Calvin traced it with radioactive carbon (¹⁴C) in the alga *Chlorella*. The first stable product is the three-carbon **3-phosphoglyceric acid (PGA)**, so this is the **C3 cycle**. It occurs in **all** photosynthetic plants.

**Stages:**
1. **Carboxylation** — CO₂ combines with the five-carbon acceptor **RuBP** (ribulose 1,5-bisphosphate) to give two PGA; catalysed by **RuBisCO**.
2. **Reduction** — PGA is converted to **triose phosphate (G3P)** using **ATP and NADPH**.
3. **Regeneration** — most G3P is rearranged to regenerate **RuBP**, using **ATP**. A small part leaves the cycle to make glucose, sucrose and starch.

**Energy and carbon bookkeeping:** each CO₂ fixed needs **3 ATP and 2 NADPH**. One glucose needs **6 turns**: **18 ATP and 12 NADPH**. In six turns, 6 RuBP (30 C) and 6 CO₂ give 12 PGA; 12 G3P are formed; **2** leave (6 C, one glucose) and **10** regenerate **6 RuBP**.

**RuBisCO** (ribulose bisphosphate carboxylase-oxygenase) is the most abundant enzyme on Earth; it is a carboxylase in the Calvin cycle and an oxygenase in photorespiration.

sections.heading: 4. C4 pathway and Kranz anatomy
sections.body_md:
In **C4 plants** (maize, sugarcane, sorghum) the first stable product is the four-carbon **oxaloacetic acid (OAA)**. The pathway was worked out by **M. D. Hatch and C. R. Slack** (Hatch and Slack pathway).

**Steps:** (1) in **mesophyll cells**, **PEP carboxylase (PEPcase)** fixes CO₂ on to **PEP** (3 C) to give **OAA** (4 C); (2) OAA is converted to **malate** (or aspartate), which moves into the **bundle sheath cells**; (3) there it is broken down to **pyruvate and CO₂**; the CO₂ enters the **Calvin cycle** (RuBisCO); (4) pyruvate returns to the mesophyll and is converted to PEP using **ATP** (2 extra ATP per CO₂). So a C4 plant needs **5 ATP and 2 NADPH per CO₂**: **30 ATP and 12 NADPH per glucose**.

**Kranz anatomy** (Kranz means wreath): large **bundle sheath cells** with many chloroplasts form a ring around each vascular bundle; mesophyll cells lie outside. The Calvin cycle is confined to the bundle sheath. The C4 pathway acts as a **CO₂ pump**, raising CO₂ around RuBisCO.

**Why C4 plants do better in hot, bright conditions:** PEPcase does not bind oxygen and has a high affinity for CO₂, so fixation continues when stomata are partly closed; CO₂ is concentrated in the bundle sheath, so RuBisCO does not act as an oxygenase and **photorespiration is negligible**; they have a higher temperature optimum and do not saturate at full sunlight.

| Feature | C3 | C4 |
|---|---|---|
| First product | PGA | OAA |
| Anatomy | no Kranz | Kranz |
| Carboxylating enzyme | RuBisCO | PEPcase, then RuBisCO |
| Photorespiration | present | negligible |
| Temperature optimum | 20–25 °C | 30–45 °C |

sections.heading: 5. Photorespiration
sections.body_md:
**Photorespiration** is the light-dependent uptake of **O₂ and release of CO₂** by the chloroplast–peroxisome–mitochondrion pathway. It occurs when **O₂ is high and CO₂ is low** (hot, bright, dry conditions in C3 plants): **RuBisCO** then acts as an **oxygenase**. RuBP + O₂ gives **one PGA** and **one phosphoglycolate** (2 C); phosphoglycolate becomes **glycolate**, which leaves the chloroplast to the **peroxisome** and becomes **glycine**; in the **mitochondrion** two glycine give **one serine, one CO₂ and ammonia**; serine returns to the chloroplast.

**Significance:** it is **wasteful**. No ATP or NADPH is made — the pathway uses them — and no sugar is made; CO₂ already fixed is lost (in the glycine step, 25 percent of the carbon of two glycolate molecules). It lowers the yield of C3 crops. It does **not** occur in C4 plants, because CO₂ is concentrated around RuBisCO in the bundle sheath. Some books say it may protect the chloroplast from light damage when CO₂ is short; this is a suggested role only.

key_terms.definition_md: Light-dependent O₂ uptake and CO₂ release by RuBisCO oxygenase activity.

sections.heading: 6. Blackman’s law of limiting factors and the factors affecting photosynthesis
sections.body_md:
**Blackman (1905):** when a process depends on several factors, its rate is limited by the factor that is **nearest its minimum value**. Raising a factor that is not limiting does not raise the rate.

**Light:** the rate rises with light intensity, then **saturates**; C3 leaves are usually light-saturated at about a tenth of full sunlight, C4 plants do not saturate in full sunlight. Quality matters (violet-blue and red are best). **CO₂:** the atmosphere has about 0.03–0.04 percent; the rate rises with CO₂ concentration, and C3 plants respond to higher CO₂ than C4 plants, which saturate lower. **Temperature:** the dark reactions are enzymatic, so the rate rises with temperature to an **optimum** and then falls as enzymes are denatured (optimum 20–25 °C for C3 and 30–45 °C for C4 plants). **Water:** a shortage closes the stomata, reducing CO₂ entry, and also affects the leaf’s water balance and enzymes.

**Graph reading (model data):** at low CO₂ the curve rises up to 40 klux and then flattens, so beyond that CO₂ is limiting; with more CO₂ the curve flattens only at 80 klux.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Saying the oxygen released comes from carbon dioxide (it comes from water).
- Mixing up absorption and action spectra.
- Drawing the Z-scheme with P700 before P680, or leaving out water, ATP or NADPH.
- Saying cyclic photophosphorylation makes NADPH (it makes only ATP).
- Giving the Calvin cycle as 3 ATP and 2 NADPH per glucose (it is per CO₂; for glucose it is 18 and 12).
- Placing the Calvin cycle of a C4 plant in the mesophyll (it is in the bundle sheath).
- Saying photorespiration makes ATP (it uses energy and makes none).

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark subparts: accessory pigment, reaction centre, enzyme, first product, a limiting factor, assertion-reason on cyclic and non-cyclic.
- 2–3-mark questions: absorption versus action spectrum; cyclic versus non-cyclic; chemiosmosis; Calvin stages; C3 versus C4; why photorespiration is wasteful.
- 5-mark questions in parts: chloroplast diagram with sites; Z-scheme with explanation; Calvin cycle with energy count; C4 pathway with Kranz anatomy.

**Assertion (A):** Xanthophylls are accessory pigments of photosynthesis.

**Reason (R):** Xanthophylls are yellow in colour.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true, but the yellow colour does not explain why xanthophylls are accessory pigments (they pass energy on and protect chlorophyll) — option (b).

answer.model_answer_md: Chlorophylls absorb mostly violet-blue and red light and reflect or transmit green light.

questions.solution_md: Green is weakly absorbed.

marking_scheme.step: Absorb blue and red, reflect green

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between an absorption spectrum and an action spectrum.

answer.model_answer_md: An **absorption spectrum** is a graph of the **amount of light absorbed** by a pigment against **wavelength**. An **action spectrum** is a graph of the **rate of photosynthesis** (for example oxygen released) against wavelength. The action spectrum follows the combined absorption of the pigments.

questions.solution_md: Definition of each.

marking_scheme.step: Absorption spectrum: light absorbed against wavelength
Action spectrum: rate of photosynthesis against wavelength

questions.stem_md: Describe how Engelmann showed which colours of light are most effective in photosynthesis.

answer.model_answer_md: He lit a filament of the alga **Cladophora**, kept in water with **aerobic bacteria**, with a **spectrum** from a prism. The bacteria collected in the **violet-blue and red** regions, where **most oxygen** was released, and were few in green. So blue and red light drive photosynthesis best.

questions.solution_md: Method and result.

marking_scheme.step: Bacteria at blue and red, so those colours are best

questions.stem_md: Name two accessory pigments of photosynthesis and state two functions that accessory pigments perform.

answer.model_answer_md: Two accessory pigments are **chlorophyll b** and **carotenoids** (or xanthophylls). They **absorb light of wavelengths** that chlorophyll a absorbs poorly and **pass the energy** to chlorophyll a; carotenoids also **protect** chlorophyll from photo-oxidation.

questions.solution_md: Two pigments; two functions.

questions.stem_md: Name the four kinds of pigment in a green leaf, state the colour of each, and say which one is the primary pigment.

answer.model_answer_md: **Chlorophyll a** is bright or blue-green and is the **primary pigment**, present in reaction centres. **Chlorophyll b** is yellow-green. **Xanthophylls** are yellow, and **carotenoids** (carotenes) are yellow to yellow-orange. Chlorophyll b, xanthophylls and carotenoids are accessory pigments that pass energy to chlorophyll a.

questions.solution_md: Four pigments, colours, primary.

questions.stem_md: Three identical Hydrilla twigs were lit for the same time through violet-blue, green and red filters of equal energy. They gave off 38, 4 and 31 bubbles per minute respectively. Which filter gave the highest rate? Why were bubbles still seen under green light, and what do the results suggest about the action spectrum?

answer.model_answer_md: The **violet-blue** filter gave the highest rate (38), closely followed by red (31). Green gave only 4, about 5.5 percent of all bubbles, because chlorophylls and accessory pigments absorb **some green light weakly**. The results suggest that the action spectrum has **peaks in blue and red** and a **low point in green**, matching absorption by the pigments.

questions.solution_md: Best filter; weak green absorption; action spectrum.

marking_scheme.step: Peaks in blue and red, trough in green

questions.stem_md:
(a) Draw a labelled diagram of a chloroplast showing the outer membrane, inner membrane, granum, stroma lamella and stroma. [2]
(b) State the part of the chloroplast in which (i) the light reaction and (ii) the Calvin cycle take place. [1]
(c) What is the function of a stroma lamella? [1]
(d) Why are the thylakoids stacked into grana? [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Diagram:** an oval chloroplast with a **double envelope** (outer and inner membrane); inside, stacks of flat **thylakoid discs** (**grana**) joined by **stroma lamellae**, all in the fluid **stroma**.

(b) (i) The light reaction takes place on the **thylakoid membranes**; (ii) the Calvin cycle takes place in the **stroma**.

(c) A **stroma lamella** joins the grana and carries **photosystem I** (cyclic photophosphorylation).

(d) Stacking gives a **large surface area** for pigments and photosystems in a small volume, so more light is absorbed.

questions.solution_md: Diagram; sites; lamella; stacking.

questions.solution_md: PS II has the reaction centre P680 — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A mutant plant makes normal reaction centres but has very few light-harvesting complexes. Compared with a normal plant, it will

options.text_md: photosynthesise much more slowly in dim light, because fewer pigment molecules pass energy to each reaction centre
photosynthesise faster in dim light, because the reaction centres are less crowded
be unable to make ATP in any light, because ATP synthase is missing
release more oxygen, because carbon dioxide is fixed by the antenna

questions.solution_md: The antenna widens the pool of absorbed light that reaches each reaction centre — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A water plant is given water made with heavy oxygen as a label, and carbon dioxide containing ordinary oxygen. The gas bubbles released in light will be found to contain the label because

options.text_md: carbon dioxide is split in the Calvin cycle and its oxygen is released
NADPH is oxidised in the stroma and gives off oxygen
water is split to replace electrons lost by photosystem II, releasing its oxygen
ATP is hydrolysed in the lumen and gives off oxygen

questions.solution_md: Water splitting at PS II releases oxygen, protons and electrons; the oxygen gas comes from water — option (c).

questions.stem_md: In isolated illuminated thylakoids, the CF₁ knobs of ATP synthase are removed but the CF₀ channels are left intact. Compared with normal thylakoids, what happens?

options.text_md: Protons build up more strongly in the lumen and ATP formation rises
Protons leak out through the open CF₀ channels and no ATP is made
Water is no longer split and NADPH formation stops at once
ATP is made in the stroma at the usual rate

questions.solution_md: CF₁ makes ATP; without it the CF₀ channel simply lets protons escape, so the gradient is lost and no ATP forms — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Stroma lamellae that lack photosystem II are isolated and illuminated. Which process can still occur in them?

options.text_md: Splitting of water with release of oxygen
Formation of NADPH using electrons from water

questions.solution_md: PS I alone supports the cyclic pathway; water splitting needs PS II and carboxylation occurs in the stroma — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A chemical makes the thylakoid membrane freely leaky to protons but does not damage the electron carriers. In illuminated thylakoids, the immediate result is that

options.text_md: electron transport continues but ATP formation falls, because the proton gradient cannot be maintained
electron transport stops at once and ATP formation rises
both electron transport and ATP formation continue unchanged
NADPH formation stops but ATP formation rises

questions.solution_md: ATP synthase depends on the gradient; the carriers still pass electrons — option (a).

questions.stem_md: The enzyme on the stroma side of the thylakoid membrane that passes electrons from ferredoxin to NADP⁺ is ______.
questions.solution_md: NADP reductase.

questions.stem_md: A preparation of illuminated thylakoids forms 60 molecules of NADPH by non-cyclic photophosphorylation. How many oxygen molecules are released? (Each NADPH takes 2 electrons; each water gives 2 electrons; one oxygen molecule comes from 2 water molecules.)
questions.solution_md: Water split $= 60$; oxygen $= 60 \div 2 = 30$.

questions.stem_md: The pH of the lumen of an illuminated thylakoid is 4.8 and that of the stroma is 7.8. By how many times is the H⁺ concentration of the lumen greater than that of the stroma?

**Assertion (A):** Cyclic photophosphorylation does not release oxygen.

**Reason (R):** Only photosystem I works in cyclic photophosphorylation, so water is not split.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are true; without PS II there is no water splitting and so no oxygen — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Cyclic photophosphorylation produces both ATP and NADPH.
questions.solution_md: False: it produces only ATP, because the electrons return to the chain instead of reaching NADP⁺.

questions.stem_md: Give a reason: No NADPH is formed in cyclic photophosphorylation.

answer.model_answer_md: The electrons from photosystem I return to the electron-transport chain instead of reaching NADP⁺.

questions.solution_md: Electrons recycled.

marking_scheme.step: Electrons return, do not reach NADP⁺

questions.stem_md: Illuminated thylakoids in beaker X make ATP and NADPH and release oxygen. Those in beaker Y make only ATP and release no oxygen. Name the pathway working in each beaker, with the photosystems involved.

answer.model_answer_md: **Beaker X** shows **non-cyclic photophosphorylation**, which needs **photosystems II and I**: water is split, giving oxygen, and the electrons end at NADP⁺ to form NADPH. **Beaker Y** shows **cyclic photophosphorylation**, which needs **photosystem I only**: the electrons return to the cytochrome complex in a loop, so only ATP is made.

questions.solution_md: Pathway and photosystems for each.

marking_scheme.step: X: non-cyclic; PS II and PS I

questions.stem_md: What is a light-harvesting complex? State its function in a photosystem.

answer.model_answer_md: A **light-harvesting complex (LHC)**, or antenna, is a group of **hundreds of chlorophyll and carotenoid molecules** bound to proteins. It **absorbs light** over a wide range and **passes the energy** to the single **reaction-centre chlorophyll a** of the photosystem.

questions.solution_md: Definition and function.

marking_scheme.step: Many pigment molecules in an antenna

questions.stem_md: Name, in order, the carriers that pass electrons from photosystem II to photosystem I in the Z-scheme.

answer.model_answer_md: Electrons from the excited reaction centre **P680** pass to **pheophytin**, then to **plastoquinone (PQ)**, then through the **cytochrome b6-f complex** to **plastocyanin (PC)**, which gives them to **P700** of photosystem I.

questions.solution_md: Order of carriers.

questions.stem_md: Explain how ATP and NADPH are formed in non-cyclic photophosphorylation.

answer.model_answer_md: Light excites **P680** of PS II, and its electrons pass down a chain (**pheophytin, plastoquinone, cytochrome b6-f, plastocyanin**) to P700. The energy released drives **ATP formation**. Light then excites **P700**; the electrons pass to **ferredoxin** and, through **NADP reductase**, to **NADP⁺**, forming **NADPH**. Electrons lost by P680 are replaced by **splitting water**, which releases oxygen.

questions.solution_md: ATP, NADPH and water splitting.

marking_scheme.step: Electron flow from PS II down the chain with ATP
PS I electrons to NADP⁺ giving NADPH

questions.stem_md: State the chemiosmotic hypothesis of ATP synthesis and give two ways in which a proton gradient is built across the thylakoid membrane.

answer.model_answer_md: According to **Mitchell’s chemiosmotic hypothesis**, ATP is made when **protons flow down a concentration gradient** through **ATP synthase**. The gradient is built (i) by the **splitting of water** on the lumen side, which releases H⁺ inside, and (ii) by **plastoquinone carrying H⁺ from the stroma into the lumen** as electrons pass; protons are also removed from the stroma by NADP reductase.

questions.solution_md: Hypothesis and two causes.

marking_scheme.step: Proton flow through ATP synthase gives ATP

questions.stem_md: The Calvin cycle needs ATP and NADPH in the ratio 3 : 2. Explain why a chloroplast may need cyclic photophosphorylation as well as the non-cyclic pathway.

answer.model_answer_md: Non-cyclic photophosphorylation makes **ATP and NADPH together**, but not enough ATP for the **3 : 2** requirement of the Calvin cycle (per carbon dioxide fixed, three ATP and two NADPH). **Cyclic photophosphorylation** makes **extra ATP without NADPH**, so the chloroplast can balance its supply to its need. It also supplies ATP when NADPH is not being used.

questions.solution_md: Balancing the ratio.

marking_scheme.step: Non-cyclic does not give enough ATP

questions.stem_md:
(a) Draw the Z-scheme of non-cyclic photophosphorylation, labelling P680, P700, plastoquinone, the cytochrome b6-f complex, plastocyanin, ferredoxin, ATP, NADPH and water splitting. [3]
(b) Name two products of the process other than ATP. [1]
(c) Why is water splitting necessary? [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Diagram:** water splitting at **PS II**; light excites **P680**; electrons fall through **pheophytin, PQ, cytochrome b6-f** (with **ATP** made) and **PC** to **P700**; light excites **P700**; electrons pass to **ferredoxin** and **NADP reductase**, giving **NADPH**; the path forms a **Z** against energy level.

(b) **NADPH** and **oxygen**.

(c) Water supplies **electrons to replace those lost by P680**, so photosystem II can keep working; it also releases **H⁺** into the lumen and **oxygen**.

questions.solution_md: Z-scheme, products, role of water.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Draw a labelled diagram of the thylakoid membrane showing PS II, the cytochrome b6-f complex, PS I, ATP synthase and the direction of H⁺ movement. [2]
(b) State three events that make the lumen rich in protons. [2]
(c) Name the two parts of ATP synthase and state the function of each. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Diagram:** a membrane with **lumen** above and **stroma** below; PS II, the **cytochrome b6-f complex**, PS I and **ATP synthase** in it; arrows showing **H⁺ entering the lumen** and flowing **out through ATP synthase**.

(b) (i) **Splitting of water** releases H⁺ in the lumen; (ii) **plastoquinone carries H⁺ from the stroma into the lumen**; (iii) **NADP reductase removes H⁺ from the stroma**, which keeps the stroma low in H⁺.

(c) **CF₀** is the **channel** through the membrane for H⁺; **CF₁** is the **knob in the stroma** that makes **ATP** from ADP and Pi.

questions.solution_md: Diagram; three causes; CF0 and CF1.

questions.solution_md: Each RuBP and CO₂ gives two PGA, so 3 × 2 = 6 — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Name the three stages of the Calvin cycle and state the product of the first stage.

answer.model_answer_md: The stages are **carboxylation**, **reduction** and **regeneration**. In **carboxylation**, carbon dioxide combines with **RuBP**, under **RuBisCO**, to give **PGA**, a three-carbon acid; this is the first stable product.

questions.stem_md: Describe the three stages of the Calvin cycle.

answer.model_answer_md: **Carboxylation:** CO₂ combines with the five-carbon acceptor **RuBP**, catalysed by **RuBisCO**, to give two molecules of three-carbon **PGA**. **Reduction:** PGA is reduced to **G3P** (triose phosphate) using **ATP and NADPH**. **Regeneration:** most G3P is rearranged to **RuBP** using **ATP**, so the cycle continues; a little G3P leaves to make sugar.

questions.solution_md: Three stages.

questions.stem_md: The Calvin cycle runs six times to make one glucose. State the number of CO₂ and RuBP molecules that enter, the number of PGA formed, and the number of G3P that leave and that regenerate RuBP.

answer.model_answer_md: 6 **CO₂** and 6 **RuBP** enter (36 carbon atoms in all), and carboxylation gives 12 **PGA**. After reduction there are 12 **G3P**, of which 2 leave the cycle to form one **glucose** (6 carbon atoms) and 10 are used, with ATP, to **regenerate 6 RuBP** (30 carbon atoms), so the cycle can continue.

questions.solution_md: Carbon bookkeeping.

answer.model_answer_md:

(b) One glucose needs **six turns** (six CO₂). Each CO₂ uses **3 ATP and 2 NADPH**, so ATP = 6 × 3 = **18** and NADPH = 6 × 2 = **12**.

questions.stem_md: Describe the C4 pathway of carbon dioxide fixation, as worked out by Hatch and Slack.

Malate moves to the **bundle sheath cells**, where it breaks down to **pyruvate and CO₂**. The CO₂ enters the **Calvin cycle**. Pyruvate returns to the mesophyll and is changed back to **PEP** using ATP.

questions.stem_md: What is photorespiration? State the condition in which RuBisCO begins this process.

answer.model_answer_md: **Photorespiration** is the **light-dependent uptake of oxygen and release of carbon dioxide** through a pathway in the **chloroplast, peroxisome and mitochondrion**, with no ATP or NADPH made. It begins when **oxygen is high and carbon dioxide is low**, and **RuBisCO acts as an oxygenase** on RuBP.

questions.stem_md: Describe the main steps of photorespiration and explain why it is considered wasteful.

answer.model_answer_md: RuBisCO adds **oxygen** to **RuBP**, giving one **PGA** and one two-carbon **phosphoglycolate**, which becomes **glycolate**. Glycolate passes to the **peroxisome** and forms **glycine**; in the **mitochondrion** two glycine give **serine and CO₂**. It is **wasteful** because **CO₂ is lost**, ATP and NADPH are used, and **no sugar** is made.

answer.model_answer_md: **Blackman’s law of limiting factors** states that when a process depends on **several factors**, its rate is determined by the factor that is **nearest its minimum value**.
